newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CLASH OF LEAGUE AND CUP DOUBLE WINNERS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CLASH OF LEAGUE AND CUP DOUBLE WINNERS.

text.p: Marseille's first division clash with Auxerre on Sunday brings together for the first time the two coaches who have most recently won the French league and cup double.
The seven-year gap between Gerard Gili's 1989 triumph with Marseille and Guy Roux's success with Auxerre this season have seen a marked contrast in the fortunes of the two French clubs.

Gili, back last year after a long absence, guided fallen giants Marseille back into the top flight from two seasons of second division purgatory following their relegation in the 1993 bribery scandal.
At the same time, Roux was enjoying his moment of greatest glory when Auxerre clinched their first league championship and second French Cup.

But seven years ago, Gili began Marseille's climb to the pinnacle of the European Cup with the first of four league titles in a row -- they were stripped of a fifth in 1993 -- and the French Cup in his first season at the helm.

Gili, at 44 Roux's junior by 14 years, retained the league title in 1990 but left the following year, refusing to work in tandem with German great Franz Beckenbauer, who had been taken on by controversial boss Bernard Tapie.
"A trainer sits on an ejector seat. At Marseille, this is no doubt even more the case than elsewhere," said Gili.
But it is not the case at Auxerre where Roux has been in charge for 35 years, taking the reins when they were a small provincial outfit with space for only 200 spectators.
Roux, 23 and a failed footballer when he began, has built a youth scheme at Auxerre to rival that of Ajax Amsterdam and an excellent scouting system.
The fruits of the consistency Roux enjoys from the Auxerre set-up where the club directors do not interfere in his work was summed up by a former player turned journalist.
"When I signed for Auxerre, Roux had been following me for nine years," said ex-striker Serge Mesones. "Today, Roux's perception is identical, only he aims higher.

"The recruiting criteria are firm. There's an archtype for being a centre-forward or a wing at Auxerre. When I see a kid, I can't say if he could play at Saint-Etienne or Paris St-Germain. At Auxerre, yes."
Roux's aim has reached so high now that he believes Auxerre's turn to win the European Cup could come before long.
"Each time I've reached a step I've turned my thoughts to the next stage," Roux said after Auxerre secured their European Cup quarter-final berth.
"We're going to take part in the quarter-finals of a European competition for the fourth time and one day it's going to be our turn (to win)."
This is new coming from a man who has tended to play down his team's stregths and objectives, a ploy he has used to some effect in casting his team as underdogs.
Big city Marseille were far from being regarded as underdogs when they flew the French flag in Europe. The fall from grace in the 1993 match-rigging scandal decimated the team.
Gili has in his squad only one survivor of Marseille's glory years, 36-year-old Jean-Philippe Durand.

Durand reflects the coach's feelings when he says: "I've been a kind of privileged witness. I took part in it all. But it's true it's difficult to go from European glory to the shadow of the second division."
They both grafted to help get Marseille back to where they believe the club belongs, the same high echelon Auxerre have reached through hard work and consistency.
